Let’s analyze the question and options step by step.  

The question asks why a sinusoidal signal is an analog signal.  

**Key definition**: An analog signal is one whose amplitude can take **any value** within a continuous range over time.  

- **(A)** *"it can have a number of values between the negative and positive peaks"* — This is correct because a sine wave’s amplitude varies continuously, taking infinitely many values between its minimum and maximum. This matches the definition of an analog signal.  

- **(B)** *"it is negative for one half cycle"* — This is true for a sine wave about zero mean, but a signal being negative part of the time doesn’t make it analog; digital signals can also represent negative numbers.  

- **(C)** *"it is positive for one half cycle"* — Same issue as (B); positivity in part of the cycle doesn’t define analog nature.  

- **(D)** *"it has positive as well as negative values"* — Again, this is a property of AC waveforms, but not the defining feature of analog signals (e.g., a square wave also has positive and negative values but can be digital if it has discrete levels).  

Only **(A)** captures the continuous amplitude property that makes a signal analog.  

Final answer: (A)
